main.summary: Cao Zhi tells a dream-like story of meeting Fufei, the goddess of the Luo river. He describes her peerless beauty, how man and goddess love each other but must part because they belong to different paths, and ends with endless regret. The language is rich and the imagination splendid, and the piece is a leading work of Wei-Jin rhapsody.
main.translation:
In the third year of Huangchu, I went to court at the capital, and on returning crossed the River Luo. The ancients have a saying that the spirit of this river is called Fufei. Moved by Song Yu's tale of the goddess, told to the King of Chu, I wrote this rhapsody. It runs:

I left the capital region, to go home to my eastern fief. I turned my back on Yique, crossed Huanyuan, passed through Tonggu and climbed Mount Jing. The sun was already sinking in the west; the carriage was spent and the horses weary. So I unyoked on a bank of fragrant asarum, fed my four horses in a field of ganoderma, strolled in the sunlit wood and let my gaze flow over the Luo.

Then my spirit shifted and my heart was startled; suddenly my thoughts scattered. Looking down I saw nothing, looking up I saw something strange: a beautiful woman, beside the rocks. I took hold of my charioteer and said to him: "Do you see anything over there? Who is she, so radiant?" The charioteer answered: "I have heard that the spirit of the Yellow River and the Luo is called Fufei. Might what my lord sees be she? What is she like? I should like to hear." I told him:

Her form is light as a startled wild goose, supple as a swimming dragon. Radiant as an autumn chrysanthemum, lush as a spring pine. Faint as a thin cloud veiling the moon, drifting as snow turned by a passing wind. Seen from afar, she is bright as the sun rising through morning mist; seen close, she glows like a lotus rising from clear waves. Plump and slender are just right, tall and short fit the measure. Her shoulders seem carved, her waist bound as with white silk. A long neck, a graceful nape, pale skin showing. No fragrant oil is added, no powder is used. Her cloud-like hair coils high; her fine brows curve and join. Red lips open bright, white teeth gleam within. Bright eyes glance well, dimples rest below the cheekbones. A rare and lovely figure, charming and free, her bearing still, her body at ease. Soft feeling and graceful manner, winning in her speech. Her dress is rare in all the age, her bones and look answer to a painting. She wears a gauze robe, shimmering, with earrings of green jade and bright pendants; on her head ornaments of gold and kingfisher feather, strung with bright pearls that light her body. She treads patterned shoes made for far journeys, and trails the light hem of misty silk. Faintly she carries the fragrance of hidden orchids, and walks lingering at the corner of the hill.

Then suddenly she let her body go free, to roam and to play. On the left she leans on coloured yak-tail banners, on the right she is shaded by cassia flags. She bares white wrists on the divine shore, to gather the dark fungus of the rapids. My heart delighted in her grace and beauty, but my spirit was shaken and ill at ease. I had no good go-between to join our joy, so I trusted the small waves to carry my words. Hoping my sincerity would arrive first, I untied my jade pendant to make my pledge. Ah, the fair one is truly refined, versed in ritual and clear in the Songs. She raised a jade pendant to answer me, and pointed to the deep pool as our meeting-place. I held my fond and earnest feelings, yet feared this spirit might deceive me. Moved by the broken pledge to Jiaofu, I stood in sad doubt and hesitation. I composed my face and stilled my will, and restated the bounds of ritual to hold myself.

Then the spirit of the Luo was moved, and wandered back and forth, undecided. Her divine light parted and joined, now dark, now bright. She lifted her light body and stood like a crane, as if to fly yet not taking wing. She trod the pepper-scented path, rich and fierce, and walked through the asarum thicket spreading fragrance. She let out a long chant of yearning, its sound sorrowful and sharp, and ever longer.

Then the host of spirits gathered in a throng, calling their companions and whistling to their mates. Some played in the clear current, some flew over the divine isle, some gathered bright pearls, some picked up kingfisher feathers. With them came the two ladies of the southern Xiang, and the roaming maidens of the Han shore. They sighed that the gourd had no mate, and sang of the Herd Boy's loneliness. She lifted her light jacket, trailing and swaying, and shaded herself with her long sleeve, standing long. Her body was swift as a flying wild duck, drifting as a spirit; she took small steps on the waves, and her silk stockings raised dust. Her movements had no fixed rule, as if in danger, as if at ease. Her advance and halt were hard to foretell, as if going, as if returning. Turning her glance, she let her spirit flow, and light shone on her jade face. Her words were held in her mouth unspoken, her breath like hidden orchids. Her lovely face, so graceful, made me forget to eat.

Then Pingyi gathered in the winds, and the Lord of the River stilled the waves. Fengyi beat the drum, and Nuwa sang clear. Patterned fish leapt up to warn the carriage, and jade bells shaped as simurghs rang as they went together. Six dragons, solemn, raised their heads in line, drawing the cloud carriage in its stately drifting. Whales leapt up on either side of the wheels, and water birds flew as an escort. Then she crossed the north islet, passed the south ridge, turned her white neck, and looked back with a clear brow. She moved her red lips and spoke slowly, setting out the main principles of our meeting. She regretted that the ways of men and spirits differ, and resented that the best years could not be matched. She raised her silk sleeve to hide her tears, which ran down her lapels in streams. She mourned that a happy meeting was gone for ever, and grieved that once she went we would be in different lands. Having no small token to show her love, she offered a bright earring from south of the Yangzi. Though she lives hidden in the deep realm of Yin, she will keep her heart with my lord for ever. Suddenly I could not tell where she had gone; I grieved as the divine night dimmed her light.

Then I turned my back on the low ground and climbed the height; my feet went on but my spirit stayed. I left my feelings to imagination, and looked back with sorrow. Hoping her spirit body would take form again, I took a light boat and went up against the current. I floated on the long river and forgot to return; my thoughts stretched on and on, and my longing grew. The night was bright and I could not sleep; I stood wet with heavy frost until dawn. I ordered my groom to ready the carriage, for I would go home by the eastern road. I took the side-horses' reins and raised the whip, and lingered sadly, unable to go.

keyLines.line: 黃初三年，余朝京師，還濟洛川
keyLines.en: In the third year of Huangchu, I went to the capital for an audience, and on returning crossed the Luo.
keyLines.note: The preface gives the occasion: in 222, after an audience in the capital, he crossed the Luo river on the road east.

keyLines.en: Light as a startled wild goose, supple as a swimming dragon.
keyLines.note: It describes the goddess's body as light as a startled wild goose and soft and graceful like a dragon on the move.

keyLines.line: 遠而望之，皎若太陽升朝霞；迫而察之，灼若芙蕖出淥波
keyLines.en: Seen from far, she is bright as the sun rising through morning mist; seen close, she glows like a lotus rising from clear waves.
keyLines.note: From afar she is bright like the sun in morning glow; near, she shines like a lotus out of the water: her beauty cannot be told in full.

keyLines.en: Shoulders as if carved, waist as if bound with white silk.
keyLines.note: Her shoulders are evenly shaped as if cut, her waist slim as if tied with white silk.

keyLines.en: Bright eyes that glance well, dimples set under the cheekbones.
keyLines.note: It describes the goddess's face: shining eyes with a charming glance, and dimples below the cheekbones.

keyLines.en: She treads lightly on the waves, and her silk stockings raise dust.
keyLines.note: The goddess walks lightly over the water and her silk stockings raise fine dust; the line became a famous way to describe a woman's light step.

keyLines.line: 恨人神之道殊兮，怨盛年之莫當
keyLines.en: I resent that the paths of man and spirit are different, and grieve that the best years cannot be matched.
keyLines.note: The paths of men and gods differ, and the fine years of youth cannot be matched: this is the key to the parting.

keyLines.line: 攬騑轡以抗策，悵盤桓而不能去
keyLines.en: I gather the reins and raise the whip, and linger sadly, unable to go.
keyLines.note: The end shows the poet pausing with his carriage, sad and unwilling to leave, leaving a long aftertaste.

glossary.note: The legendary goddess of the Luo river, said to be a daughter of Fuxi who drowned in the Luo and became a goddess.

glossary.en: Song Yu dui Chu Wang shennu shi - Song Yu's tale of the goddess for the King of Chu
glossary.note: Refers to Song Yu's 'Rhapsody on the Goddess' and 'Rhapsody on Gaotang', which tell how the King of Chu dreamed of a goddess.
To unyoke the carriage and rest; shui is the same as 'tuo', to take off.

glossary.en: nong xian de zhong, xiu duan he du - neither too plump nor too thin
glossary.note: Her plumpness and slimness, her height, are just right. Nong means full.
The powder used by women in ancient times.
The legendary water god of the Yellow River.

main.background: Cao Zhi was the son of Cao Cao and the younger brother of Cao Pi, a poet of the Wei and Jin period. He wrote this rhapsody in 222, on his way back to his fief after an audience in the capital, when he passed the Luo river. Later readers have proposed that it hides feelings about the ruler and his own disappointment, but views differ and cannot be pinned down. Gu Kaizhi based his painting 'Nymph of the Luo River' on it.
